articles.title: Welsh government pledges to end A&E corridor care by 2029
articles.summary: The Welsh government has vowed to speed up emergency care and help patients get home sooner.
articles.body:
A patient spent more than two days waiting in A&E on two separate occasions - and has vowed never to go back.

Andrew Railton, 63, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, said he sat "on the same chair" at Royal Glamorgan Hospital, in Talbot Green, for more than 50 hours on each visit after suffering from pneumonia, and then "deathly low" potassium levels.

It comes as a £23m plan by the Welsh government promises to end A&E corridor care in Wales by 2029.

Senior emergency doctors have warned too many patients in Wales are experiencing "a terrible time" due to emergency care pressures and delays.

Cwm Taf Morgannwg health board said it was sorry for Railton's experience and the distress caused.

Railton said he was "pretty poorly" and sat in the waiting room for around nine hours before seeing a doctor.

"I was put in the chair and obviously put on the drip... but basically sat in this draughty corridor," he said.

"They brought stools and chairs, and there were people basically just stood around all over the place with drips in them, and it was something Victorian. I was there for 50-odd hours."

A bed was eventually found for him and he stayed in hospital for a further three days.

But a few months later he was told to go back to A&E because of "deathly low" potassium levels.

"Believe it or not, I was put in exactly the same chair that I was in last time. And I sat in that chair overnight while I had a drip administered to me," he said.

Railton says there is "no chance in hell" of him going back to the A&E even if his "leg falls off".

The Welsh government's new emergency care plan points to delays and problems in 2025-26:

Ambulances took an average of two hours and 24 minutes from arrival in hospital to transferring their patients, resulting in 184,850 "lost hours"

Patients aged 85 or over spent an average of seven hours and 13 minutes in A&E with 15% of all cases waiting more than 12 hours

62,346 people admitted as an emergency stayed more than 21 days in hospital

There are around 1,400 patients, at any given time, occupying beds that are clinically ready to leave

With each bed occupied costing £500-£600 a day, the bill to the NHS was £172m

The new plan sets goals for the "whole journey" of the patient - from the scene of the emergency, through to recovery at home.

One of the key milestones is that A&E corridor care or care in other unsuitable spaces should be eliminated by 2029.

Mabon ap Gwynfor, Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, said: "When someone needs emergency care, they should know help will come quickly, they will receive the right care, and they will spend only as long in hospital as they need to.

"Too many people do not experience this consistently today and that must change."

Emergency doctors have frequently warned that patients too often face harm because they are being treated in unsafe spaces in A&E.

Speaking to Politics Wales, Dr Katja Empson, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, warned that too many patients were experiencing "terrible" conditions.

"They're often spending a very long time waiting for a bed, and often in a very inappropriate area," she said.

"We are causing harm because people are delayed in the emergency department."

The plan sets out an "ambition" to discharge patients from hospital, where possible, within 72 hours.

It includes making sure patients get early assessments from a senior clinicians, receive quick diagnostic tests and get rapid support from pharmacy and therapy and rehabilitation teams.

Planning for a safe transfer home should happen from the moment a patient arrives, the plan says.

The plan also aims to address relatively poor survival rates for people having cardiac arrests in communities.

It notes that of the 2,800 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occur each year - just one in 20 in Wales (5%) survive compared to 8% in England and 10% in Scotland.

There is an ambition for Wales to become a "nation of life-savers" by 2029 by training people to be more confident in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and raising awareness among children and young people.

New technology will be explored such as drones carrying defibrillators that can save lives.

The "nation of life-savers" aim is supported by Ed Grant, a Welsh Ambulance community first responder who was himself saved by CPR.

The 73-year-old from Barry spent 50 years volunteering in various emergency services.

"I'm actually living proof that CPR works," he said, recalling how his wife kept him alive after he suffered a cardiac arrest at home three years ago.

"Luckily my wife knows CPR because I taught her... she started CPR on me, called the ambulance and called one of my responders as well."

He said community responders can often reach patients first, particularly in rural areas.

"We work very much in tandem with the ambulance service... we can get there first and start dealing with it, keep the person alive and well until the ambulance can arrive," he said.

The plan will include new set of measures and targets which will be recorded and reported on annually from spring next year, with a review in 2030.

These will include measures of patient survival and recovery as well as people's experience of care including corridor care.

Dr Siobhan Lewis, National Clinical Lead for Frailty in NHS Wales and consultant geriatrician, said: "We are already seeing the effects of an ageing population and those living with multiple medical conditions in our acute care areas, and the need for person-centred care has never been greater."

articles.title: Pancreatic cancer mystery deepens as researchers make unexpected discovery
articles.summary: University of Cincinnati study found Black patients' pancreatic tumors had more B cells and cells tied to drug resistance, pointing to tailored care.
articles.body: A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently, potentially leading to more personalized treatments. Researchers examined 22 pancreatic tumors from patients of different racial backgrounds across the U.S., looking for differences in cancer cells and how the immune system responds to them. The study included seven Black patients and 15 non-African American patients. The findings were published in the journal Cancer Research. FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE Tumors from Black patients had fewer of the most common type of pancreatic cancer cells and more cells with a mix of different characteristics, the researchers found. Some of those cell characteristics have been associated with drug resistance, but the study did not establish whether they affected patients’ treatment outcomes. Additionally, tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer, although the significance of these differences is unclear. PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said that using immunotherapy to help the immune system attack the disease has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer. "That's been very difficult to do in pancreatic cancer because the pancreatic tumor subverts the immune system so that it is fighting for it instead of for the host or the rest of the body," Wadlow, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. The study found no significant differences between groups in the major genetic changes known to drive the disease. Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers. WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS The findings highlight the importance of including patients from different backgrounds in cancer research, according to lead study author Nina Steele, Ph.D., an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine. "This study shows that ignoring diverse ancestry in medical research leaves blind spots in the search for a cure," she told Fox News Digital. Wadlow noted that pancreatic cancers can share major DNA mutations but can differ considerably in how their cells behave and interact with nearby immune cells and surrounding tissue. "Those differences may also vary across patient populations, such as between Black and non-Black patients," he told Fox News Digital. "While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care." "That is potentially important both for understanding disparities in pancreatic cancer and, ultimately, for developing more individualized treatments." Pancreatic cancer can vary from one tumor to another, and even within the same tumor, Wadlow explained. "The cancer cell itself is only part of the story," he said. The surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment, helping to explain why a single treatment approach may not work for every patient. The findings have several limitations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Researchers have not established how the intermediate tumor cells affect survival or whether they respond differently to standard chemotherapy, Steele said. The team also needs to study pancreatic tissue from people without cancer to better understand when these differences develop. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Wadlow cautioned that race and genetic ancestry do not fully account for the environmental, socioeconomic and biological factors that could explain the findings. Larger studies involving patients from diverse backgrounds are needed to determine whether these differences affect treatment outcomes or survival, the oncologist said. "While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care," he added. Wadlow encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If we find an inherited mutation, then family members can be tested," he said. Steele said the findings also underscore the need for clinical trials that represent the patients affected by pancreatic cancer. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It is also a reminder for the medical system to ensure that clinical trials reflect the entire population at risk, in order to find treatments that can help all patients, not just some patients," she told Fox News Digital. The research was funded in part by the National Cancer Institute.

articles.title: Haven’t Exercised in a While? This Is the Best Time of Day to Go for a Walk
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, an orthopedic surgeon reveals the best time of day to walk if you’re starting from zero in order to maximize the health benefits.
articles.body: If you’re starting a new fitness journey or getting back into exercise after a long break, you’re not alone. Everyone has to begin somewhere, even if it’s just getting up off the couch. And if you’re starting from zero, walking is one of the best ways to move your body and improve your physical fitness, orthopedic surgeon Dr. Vonda Wright tells TODAY.com. Walking is an accessible, low-impact and science-backed way to boost both physical and mental health. If you’re a beginner, you may set out to walk a certain distance or number of steps at first. But the time of day you choose to go on a walk also matters, says Wright. In order to get the most out of your walk, Wright recommends walking at a specific time of day. Fitness Tip of the Day: Go on A Walk After Eating Your Largest Meal of the Day “...Take a walk after your biggest meal,” says Wright. Whether that’s breakfast, lunch or dinner, try to go on your walk within about 30 minutes to an hour of finishing eating. Why It Matters Going on a walk after eating your largest meal of the day has several advantages, especially if you’re switching from a formerly sedentary lifestyle. Approximately 25% of Americans report getting zero physical activity outside of work, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Walking is a tremendous way to start moving, says Wright, and strategically timing your walk can maximize the benefits. Going on a walk will get the muscles moving, heart rate up and lungs working harder, which improves cardiovascular health. Activating the muscles, especially the large muscle groups in the lower body, also helps pull glucose out of the bloodstream. And after a meal is when blood sugar tends to spike the highest. Research shows that walking for just two to five minutes after a meal can help manage blood sugar and insulin levels, TODAY.com previously reported. Walking after eating can also aid digestion by speeding up gastrointestinal motility, or the transit time of food moving through our digestive system. Finally, a walk can combat feelings of sluggishness after a large meal, which may help boost mood. How To Get Started If you’re truly starting from zero, Wright recommends walking for just five minutes at first. “Then go up to ten minutes, and eventually work your way up to 30 minutes,” Wright recommends. The ultimate goal should be to walk for at least 30 minutes at a moderate-intensity pace, most days of the week. If you want to make your walks more challenging, try increasing the time or distance, speeding up your pace, walking at an incline or wearing a weighted vest, says Wright. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Jaipur cafe owner beaten with rods on way home dies after 11 days; 3 held
articles.summary: Jaipur Vaishali Nagar cafe owner Mayank Gopaliya dies 11 days after assault; police arrest three men after dispute over employee’s friend visiting cafe.
articles.body: JAIPUR: A cafe owner who was brutally assaulted near his shop in Vaishali Nagar on Nov 5 died in hospital late Monday night, 11 days after the attack. Police have arrested three men for the assault, which allegedly stemmed from the owner’s objection to a female employee’s friend frequenting the cafe.Mayank Gopaliya, who ran a bakery and cafe on Vaishali Marg and lived in Vaishali Nagar, was attacked around 9:45 pm while walking home after closing his cafe. Two men allegedly ran towards him from behind and repeatedly struck him with sticks and rods. He collapsed after being hit on the head.The attackers fled with their associates, who were waiting on a motorcycle and a scooter, after assuming Gopaliya was dead. He suffered serious head injuries and underwent surgery. He died during treatment at a private hospital late Monday night. His body was shifted to Jaipuria Hospital mortuary for post-mortem.Police have arrested Mohammad Shahrukh, Akman and Mohammad Rashid alias Altamash in connection with the attack. Investigators said Shahrukh often visited the cafe to meet a woman employee. Mayank had objected to this, following which Shahrukh allegedly threatened to kill him.A quarrel took place between them on Nov 5. articles.title: The US Has Lost Its Measles Elimination Status, and These States Are the Biggest Hotspots. See the Map
articles.summary: Measles is now endemic in the U.S. after being eliminated. Here’s which states are reporting the most cases.
articles.body: Measles, a vaccine-preventable disease once considered eliminated in the United States, has been surging across the country in recent months. Amid record-breaking outbreaks, the U.S. has officially lost its measles elimination status, which it held for over 26 years. Also known as rubeola, measles is a viral respiratory disease that causes fever, coughing, a runny nose and a characteristic blotchy red rash. If left untreated, measles can lead to pneumonia, swelling of the brain and death, per the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Measles is especially dangerous for young children. It’s airborne and widely considered one of the most contagious viruses in the world. Once a common childhood illness in the U.S., measles can be prevented with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective, per the CDC. Thanks to successful immunization efforts, measles was considered eliminated in the U.S. in 2000. After decades of progress, measles is now spreading continuously nationwide. The resurgence of measles in the U.S. and globally is being fueled by falling childhood vaccination rates, experts say. Here’s what to know about measles in the U.S. US Loses Measles Elimination Status The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional office for the Americas of the World Health Organization (WHO), announced on Tuesday that the U.S. had officially lost its measles elimination status. Measles is now considered endemic in the U.S. after “showing sustained transmission for more than 12 months,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, said in a press briefing on Nov. 17. In addition to the U.S., Mexico also had its measles elimination status withdrawn this week. Canada lost its status in 2025. The Americas have reported some 58,000 cases total this year alone, compared to less than 15,000 in 2025, per PAHO. “These figures are a serious warning for our region,” Barbosa said. The U.S. losing its measles elimination status after 26 years has sparked alarm among many public health experts. “I’m certainly disappointed and concerned. We were the leaders in the world demonstrating that you could actually eliminate measles, and now we’ve slipped back,” Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, tells TODAY.com. “It’s like getting a report card. Years ago, we had an A. Now we’re getting an F,” Schaffner adds. “The United States has an extraordinary measles problem. We’ve had more measles cases in the last 18 months than we’ve had in the previous 25 years combined,” Noel Brewer, a professor of public health the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told NBC News. Measles Cases in the U.S. As of Nov. 12, there have been 5,412 confirmed measles cases reported in the U.S. since the start of 2026, according to the CDC. Among these cases, 591 people have been hospitalized. As of Nov. 17, 10 measles-related deaths have been reported by state health departments: seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin and one in New York. The CDC has confirmed 6 deaths from measles this year to date. At least 45 states and the District of Columbia have reported measles cases in 2026, per the CDC: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Pennsylvania accounts for the lion’s share of measles cases so far this year with a case count of 1,529 as of Nov. 12, per CDC data. South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have also reported more than 500 measles cases since the start of 2026. Only five states have reported zero confirmed measles cases so far this year, per the latest CDC data: Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, Nevada and New Hampshire. Children and teenagers account for many of the measles cases in the U.S. “It’s causing about one in 10 children to be hospitalized,” says Schaffner. Map of Measles Hotspots So far in 2026, the CDC has confirmed at least 43 measles outbreaks nationwide. “We are having many outbreaks, some larger and smaller, throughout the United States,” says Schaffner. Here are the biggest measles hot spots in the U.S., according to an NBC News analysis of the most recent CDC data: Pennsylvania is currently seeing the nation’s largest outbreak. “We are seeing this outbreak now because of a failure to vaccinate. This virus is very serious. It can be deadly. It can cause a lot of pain and a lot of suffering, and I’m seeing that every day,” Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease expert in Pennsylvania, told TODAY in a Nov. 17 segment. MMR Vaccination Rates Are Falling The MMR vaccine is safe and effective, says Schaffner. Two doses, given at 12-15 months and 4-6 years of age, are 97% effective. “When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through herd immunity,” the CDC says. This indirectly protects vulnerable individuals who can’t get vaccinated, such as newborns or pregnant women. However, childhood MMR vaccination rates have fallen below the 95% threshold in recent years, and they keep declining. During the 2025-2026 school year, only 92% of U.S. kindergarteners had been vaccinated against measles, per CDC data. Gaps in vaccination coverage can allow the virus to spread, leading to outbreaks. “We could get back to measles being at zero if parents would take their children to be vaccinated,” says Schaffner. Can You Get Measles If You’re Vaccinated? While exceptionally rare, it is possible to contract measles after you’ve been vaccinated, TODAY.com reported previously. Most people who are fully vaccinated against measles are considered to have lifelong immunity to the virus. Still, the MMR vaccine is 97% effective — which means roughly 3 in 100 people who get both doses can still get measles if exposed. Among the confirmed measles cases reported in the U.S. this year, only 2% had received both doses, per CDC data. However, the chances of getting measles after two doses of the MMR vaccine are still “extraordinarily low,” Schaffner previously told TODAY.com. When breakthrough infections do happen, they tend to be milder. There are no recorded cases of a healthy, fully vaccinated person dying from measles, according to TODAY.com reporting. Who Needs the Measles Vaccine? The CDC recommends all children get two doses of the MMR vaccine to protect against measles, starting at 12 months of age. “My advice would be for parents to speak with their pediatricians about vaccinating their children against measles,” says Schaffner. If you aren’t sure whether you’re fully vaccinated, you can request your immunization records from your doctor. People who were born before 1957, when measles was rampant, likely acquired immunity through infection, says Schaffner. The measles vaccine became available in 1963, but some people born between 1963 and 1968 may have received an earlier, less effective version of the vaccine or only one dose. “If your measles vaccination history is a little blurry, you can just get another dose of vaccine. There’s absolutely no harm in that,” says Schaffner.

articles.title: Preocupación por la salud de Norberto Peluffo: piden urgente donantes de sangre
articles.standfirst: Familiares piden donantes de sangre de urgencia en Bucaramanga
articles.summary: Familiares piden donantes de sangre de urgencia en Bucaramanga
articles.body: El balompié nacional se une en una sola voz de aliento y apoyo. En las últimas horas, los familiares de Norberto Peluffo, figura histórica del fútbol colombiano, exjugador profesional y reconocido analista deportivo, lanzaron un llamado urgente a la ciudadanía para conseguir donantes de sangre en la ciudad de Bucaramanga. La noticia ha sacudido a los seguidores del deporte rey, y a gran parte de aficionados en Colombia donde el 'Mono' Peluffo se ha ganado el cariño y el respeto gracias a su impecable labor como técnico y posteriormente comentarista en Copas del Mundo, Eliminatorias y torneos sudamericanos. De acuerdo con la información entregada por su entorno cercano y medios locales, Norberto Peluffo, de 67 años y oriundo de tierra santandereana, ha venido afrontando quebrantos de salud desde el primer semestre de este 2026. Tras más de seis meses bajo rigurosos tratamientos médicos para combatir una delicada enfermedad, el estado de salud del exentrenador ha requerido una atención prioritaria. Pese a lo complejo del panorama, quienes han tenido la oportunidad de conversar recientemente con él destacan su entereza y optimismo, afirmando que se mantiene aferrado a su "fe en Dios" para salir adelante de este difícil trance personal. Su actitud abierta, amable y su característico don de gente han permanecido intactos a pesar de las adversidades médicas. Ante la urgencia del requerimiento clínico, la familia ha hecho un llamado enfático a los ciudadanos de Bucaramanga y su área metropolitana que deseen y puedan colaborar con esta causa humanitaria. Tipo de sangre requerido: O+ (O positivo). Lugar de donación: Laboratorios Higuera Escalante, ubicados en Bucaramanga. Cualquier persona que cumpla con los requisitos habituales para la donación de sangre y cuente con este tipo sanguíneo puede acercarse al centro médico mencionado para aportar su granito de arena en la recuperación de una de las personalidades más queridas del deporte nacional. Norberto Peluffo dejó una huella profunda en el fútbol profesional colombiano, tanto dentro como fuera de las canchas. Como jugador: Durante las décadas de los 80 y 90, se consolidó como un talentoso volante, vistiendo las camisetas de instituciones de gran tradición como Millonarios, Atlético Nacional y América de Cali, además de ser referente del Atlético Bucaramanga. Su visión de juego y liderazgo en el terreno de juego lo catapultaron como un referente de su época. Como director técnico: En su etapa desde el banquillo, dirigió a varios de los equipos más importantes del país, imprimiendo su conocimiento táctico y su rigor profesional. Como analista y comunicador: En los últimos años, el 'Mono' se consolidó como una de las voces más analíticas y respetadas de los medios de comunicación en Colombia. Además de su rol fundamental en las transmisiones de Gol Caracol al lado de Javier Hernández Bonnet. La comunidad deportiva, colegas, amigos y seguidores continúan enviando mensajes de solidaridad y pronta recuperación a un hombre que le ha entregado su vida al fútbol con pasión y decencia. Hoy, el partido más importante lo juega por su salud, y la ciudadanía tiene la oportunidad de asistirlo desde las gradas de la solidaridad.

articles.title: Cork: Two arrested after murder in the city
articles.summary: Two males have been arrested after a man in his late teens was murdered in Cork City in the Republic of Ireland.
articles.body:
A murder investigation has commenced after a man in his late teens died following an assault in Cork city in the Republic of Ireland.

Gardaí (Irish police) said the man sustained critical wounds during the assault at Lower Glanmire Road at about 13:30 local time on Tuesday, which Irish broadcaster RTÉ has reported was a stabbing.

He was transferred to Cork University Hospital for urgent medical attention, where he later died.

Two males, an adult teenager and a juvenile, have been arrested in connection with the investigation, gardai said.

A post-mortem will be carried out on Wednesday at Cork University Hospital.

The investigation is being coordinated from an incident room at Mayfield Garda Station under the direction of a Senior Investigating Officer.

Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

articles.title: Mulher morre e outras 14 recebem atendimento médico após tumulto em inauguração de loja no MA; VÍDEO | G1
articles.standfirst: Tumulto aconteceu na manhã desta quarta-feira (18), em Bacabal. Segundo a prefeitura, estabelecimento não tinha alvará de funcionamento.
articles.summary: Tumulto aconteceu na manhã desta quarta-feira (18), em Bacabal. Segundo a prefeitura, estabelecimento não tinha alvará de funcionamento.
articles.body:
Uma mulher morreu e outras 14 pessoas precisaram de atendimento médico após um tumulto durante a inauguração de uma loja popular, na manhã desta quarta-feira (18), em Bacabal , no Maranhão. Um vídeo mostra o momento em que uma multidão se empurra, derruba os portões do estabelecimento e entra na loja ( veja o vídeo acima ).

Nas imagens, dezenas de pessoas aparecem aglomeradas em frente à loja. Em meio à confusão, os portões são derrubados e parte da multidão avança para dentro do estabelecimento. Durante o tumulto, pessoas foram pisoteadas.

Algumas pessoas passaram a noite na fila para aproveitar a inauguração da loja, que anunciava diversos produtos por R$ 10 , incluindo eletrodomésticos, como liquidificadores e ventiladores .

Durante o tumulto, uma mulher sofreu ferimentos graves na cabeça após ser pisoteada e outra teve o peito perfurado por uma estrutura do portão. Uma terceira mulher passou mal durante a confusão, precisou ser intubada e morreu após ser encaminhada ao hospital. A causa da morte ainda não foi informada .

Segundo a Prefeitura de Bacabal, 15 pessoas precisaram de atendimento médico. Quatro vítimas, incluindo a mulher que morreu, foram encaminhadas em estado grave ao Hospital Estadual Laura Vasconcelos.

As outras 11 pessoas foram atendidas no Hospital Geral de Bacabal (Socorrão), sem apresentar quadro grave. Dessas, quatro permanecem em avaliação médica e passam por exames.

Mulher morre e 14 pessoas são atendidas após tumulto em inauguração de loja no MA — Foto: Reprodução

Segundo a Prefeitura de Bacabal, o estabelecimento não possuía alvará de funcionamento . O prefeito Roberto Costa ( MDB ) determinou o fechamento imediato da loja após tomar conhecimento do tumulto.

A administração municipal informou ainda que o Cadastro Nacional da Pessoa Jurídica (CNPJ) apresentado pelo estabelecimento está registrado em Alto Alegre do Maranhão , sob outra denominação.

O Corpo de Bombeiros também esteve no local e constatou que a loja não possuía certificado de segurança emitido pela corporação. O estabelecimento foi interditado .

Equipes da Saúde, da Assistência Social e da Guarda Municipal foram mobilizadas para atender às vítimas.

Em nota, a loja lamentou o ocorrido, afirmou que não tem responsabilidade pelo tumulto e declarou que vai colaborar com as autoridades para prestar esclarecimentos e evitar situações semelhantes .

A Prefeitura de Bacabal informou que adotará medidas para apurar os fatos e buscar a responsabilização dos envolvidos. A administração municipal também afirmou que presta assistência social e psicológica às vítimas e aos familiares.

articles.title: Suspeito de matar enteada com golpe de enxada após assédio é preso  | G1
articles.standfirst: Maely Delfino Amaro, de 63 anos, foi preso nesta terça-feira (17). Phâmella Barbosa Silva, de 23 anos, morreu no hospital no domingo (15). Segundo familiares, homem tentou olhar a jovem enquanto ela tomava banho antes de atacá-la.
articles.summary: Phâmella Barbosa Silva, de 23 anos, foi agredida em Itapemirim, no Sul do estado. Segundo familiares, homem tentou olhar a jovem enquanto ela tomava banho antes de atacá-la.
articles.body:
Maely Delfino Amaro, de 63 anos, suspeito de matar a ex-enteada Phâmella Barbosa Silva , de 23 anos, com golpes de enxada, em Itapemirim , no Sul do Espírito Santo, foi preso na manhã desta terça-feira (17) . O crime aconteceu no último domingo (15) , na localidade de Ilha do Gato.

O suspeito estava foragido desde o dia do crime. Segundo testemunhas, ele usou uma enxada para atingir a cabeça de Phâmella. A jovem chegou a ser socorrida, mas morreu horas depois na Santa Casa de Misericórdia de Cachoeiro de Itapemirim.

Policiais militares, civis e agentes da Guarda Civil realizaram buscas pelo suspeito durante o domingo e a segunda-feira (16), mas ele não havia sido localizado.

Phâmella Barbosa Silva, de 23 anos, foi morta com golpes de enxada pelo padrasto no Espírito Santo — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Segundo a Polícia Civil, havia um mandado de prisão temporária contra o homem, expedido pelo Poder Judiciário após representação do delegado responsável pelo caso.

Ele se apresentou à delegacia no início da manhã desta terça-feira, acompanhado de um advogado. O homem é investigado por feminicídio.

A jovem Phâmella Barbosa Silva, de 23 anos, atingida por golpes de enxada na cabeça pelo próprio padrasto , de 63 anos, em Itapemirim, no Sul do Espírito Santo, morreu no hospital na noite deste domingo (15). A agressão aconteceu na localidade de Ilha do Gato, na manhã do mesmo dia.

Segundo o relato de um familiar à polícia, o homem dava em cima da jovem, mas ela não correspondia às investidas. No domingo, ele teria tentado olhar a enteada enquanto ela tomava banho. A situação provocou uma discussão.

A mãe da jovem tentou separar os dois. Durante a briga, Phâmella foi jogada contra um muro e caiu. Nesse momento, o padrasto teria atingido a cabeça dela com golpes de enxada.

Homem dá golpes de enxada na cabeça da enteada e foge em Itapemirim, no Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação

A vítima foi socorrida por duas pessoas em um veículo particular e levada inicialmente ao Hospital Evangélico Litoral Sul. Depois, foi encaminhada à Santa Casa de Cachoeiro de Itapemirim, na mesma região, onde permaneceu internada em estado gravíssimo.

De acordo com a Polícia Militar, os policiais foram acionados para atender a uma ocorrência de tentativa de homicídio. Quando chegaram ao endereço, não encontraram a vítima nem o suspeito.

Na residência, os militares localizaram uma enxada ensanguentada e marcas de sangue espalhadas pelo chão e pela varanda.

As equipes fizeram buscas na casa, no quintal e nas proximidades, mas não conseguiram localizar o homem. Outras viaturas também realizaram patrulhamento na região.

A jovem não morava no imóvel. Segundo familiares, a mãe dela e o suspeito eram separados, mas continuavam vivendo na mesma residência.

O caso foi encaminhado à Delegacia de Polícia Judiciária de Itapemirim. A Polícia Civil informou que a investigação ficará a cargo da Delegacia Regional do município.

A jovem Phâmella Barbosa Silva, de 23 anos, atingida por golpes de enxada na cabeça em Itapemirim, no Sul do Espírito Santo, morreu no hospital — Foto: Reprodução/Rede social

articles.title: Batida entre carro e ambulância atropela pedestre em Nova Friburgo | G1
articles.standfirst: Colisão aconteceu na terça-feira (17), na Avenida Comte Bittencourt; motorista de carro e pedestre ficaram feridos e foram levados ao Hospital Raul Sertã.
articles.summary: Colisão aconteceu na terça-feira (17), na Avenida Comte Bittencourt; motorista de carro e pedestre ficaram feridos e foram levados ao Hospital Raul Sertã.
articles.body:
Colisão entre carro e ambulância atropela um pedestre em Nova Friburgo. — Foto: Eliandra Bussinger

Uma batida entre um carro e uma ambulância do Samu deixou duas pessoas feridas em Nova Friburgo , Região Serrana do Rio, na terça-feira (17). O acidente aconteceu por volta de 13h30, na Avenida Comte Bittencourt, no Centro da cidade.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, a colisão atingiu um pedestre que passava pela calçada no momento da batida. Com o impacto, o carro ficou bastante amassado.

De acordo com os agentes, a motorista do veículo e o pedestre atropelado, um funcionário de um mercado que carregava compras no momento do acidente, sofreram ferimentos leves e foram encaminhados para o Hospital Raul Sertã.

O paciente que era transportado pela ambulância também foi levado ao hospital. Segundo os bombeiros, ele vinha de Lumiar e não se feriu no acidente, tendo sido encaminhado à unidade apenas para continuidade do atendimento médico.

O acidente voltou a chamar a atenção para a segurança no trecho da Avenida Comte Bittencourt, uma das vias com maior circulação de veículos e pedestres no Centro de Nova Friburgo, especialmente no início da tarde.

Há menos de uma semana, a morte do comerciante Jorge Duarte, atropelado por uma bicicleta na mesma avenida, foi tema de reportagens nos jornais da cidade. O novo caso reforça a preocupação com os acidentes registrados no local.

Com a colisão o carro ficou com a traseira e a porta do motorista amassados. — Foto: Eliandra Bussinger

articles.title: Sarampo nos EUA: país perde status de erradicação após 26 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Os Estados Unidos notificaram mais de 5,4 mil casos e 10 mortes relativas ao sarampo, pela primeira vez desde o início dos anos 1990.
articles.summary: A Opas revogou o certificado de erradicação do sarampo nos EUA após o país registrar 5,4 mil casos e 10 mortes, o maior índice desde o início dos anos 1990.
articles.body:
Por que EUA perderam certificado de eliminação do sarampo após 26 anos — Foto: Getty Images / BBC

Após mais de duas décadas, os Estados Unidos perderam o status de país livre do sarampo, em meio a dois anos de recordes nos números de casos e mortes.

A Organização Pan-Americana da Saúde (Opas), um serviço especializado das Nações Unidas, concluiu que houve nos EUA transmissão ininterrupta da mesma linhagem do vírus do sarampo por mais de 12 meses.

O diretor da Opas, Jarbas Barbosa, anunciou que o México e a Bolívia também perderam seu status de erradicação do sarampo. Ele atribuiu o ressurgimento da doença no continente a "falhas de vacinação" persistentes.

Os Centros de Controle e Prevenção de Doenças dos Estados Unidos (CDC, na sigla em inglês) afirmaram estar comprometidos com a "reobtenção do status de erradicação do sarampo", ampliando o acesso às vacinas.

Os Estados Unidos registraram 5,4 mil casos de sarampo apenas este ano, com 10 mortes relacionadas à doença. Este é o maior número já observado no país desde os anos 1990.

O sarampo (com suas erupções vermelhas características) costumava infectar milhões de crianças por ano antes da invenção da vacina.

O vírus é extremamente contagioso, pode ser fatal e alguns pacientes podem sofrer complicações de longo prazo, como encefalite e amnésia imune, que reinicia o sistema imunológico, limitando a capacidade do paciente de reagir a novas infecções.

Os Estados Unidos recomendam duas doses da vacina tríplice viral (que protege contra o sarampo, a caxumba e a rubéola) em crianças de um a seis anos de idade, o que oferece 97% de proteção contra a doença.

A Opas tomou a decisão de revogar o status de erradicação do sarampo nos Estados Unidos ao constatar que o vírus circulou de forma ininterrupta no país por mais de um ano.

"Estes números são um sério alerta para a nossa região", declarou Barbosa em entrevista coletiva, nesta terça-feira (17/11). "O sarampo está ressurgindo em todo o mundo, em meio a persistentes falhas de vacinação."

Ele destacou que o Canadá, que perdeu seu status de erradicação do sarampo no ano passado após vários grandes surtos, realizou progressos este ano para interromper o contágio.

O gerente-executivo de imunizações da Opas, Daniel Salas, afirmou que os Estados Unidos e outros países que perderam o status de erradicação precisarão apresentar planos de ações corretivas, descrevendo como eles tentarão aumentar os índices de vacinação.

O secretário de Saúde dos Estados Unidos, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., tentou estabelecer diversas mudanças radicais das recomendações e políticas americanas de vacinação.

Cético em relação à vacina, ele lançou frequentemente dúvidas sobre a segurança da vacina tríplice viral, enquanto os índices de vacinação caíam nos Estados Unidos nos últimos anos.

Kennedy defendeu que o aumento dos casos de sarampo começou antes que ele assumisse o cargo e que países vizinhos também observaram maior número de infecções.

Em resposta ao anúncio desta terça-feira, os CDC afirmaram que o organismo e seus parceiros "estão comprometidos a interromper os surtos de sarampo, proteger os americanos e obter novamente o status de erradicação do sarampo".

"Juntos, incentivaremos a vacina tríplice viral, ampliaremos o acesso às vacinas e ajudaremos as comunidades a eliminar lacunas de proteção", declararam os CDC.

A diretora do organismo, Erica Schwartz, afirmou que a designação de país livre do sarampo não é o que protege os cidadãos americanos.

"O que protege é a vacinação", segundo ela. "Sabemos onde está ocorrendo a transmissão e investimos US$ 100 milhões [cerca de R$ 580 milhões] em departamentos de saúde estaduais e regionais para atingir estas comunidades."

O Reino Unido, a Espanha e a Áustria são algumas das nações europeias que perderam seus status de países livres do sarampo no início deste ano, ao lado de países como a Rússia, o Azerbaijão e o Uzbequistão.

O professor de medicina Nuwan Gunawardhana, do Centro Médico Irving da Universidade Colúmbia, nos Estados Unidos, declarou que a perda do status de erradicação pelos Estados Unidos é "um enorme passo atrás".

Os EUA foram o primeiro país a erradicar o sarampo no continente americano, graças às campanhas de vacinação, segundo o especialista em doenças infecciosas pediátricas William Moss, da Escola de Saúde Pública Bloomberg da Universidade Johns Hopkins, nos Estados Unidos.

Gunawardhana afirmou que foram necessários imensos esforços das autoridades de saúde pública e dos médicos para estabelecer a confiança dos pacientes e aumentar a adoção da vacina tríplice viral, levando a baixos números de infecções e mortes nos Estados Unidos por décadas.

Mas esta confiança vem diminuindo sistematicamente desde a pandemia de covid-19, quando, segundo o médico, os pacientes receberam desinformações sobre a segurança das vacinas e chegaram a perder ainda mais confiança nos sistemas de saúde pública.

Com isso, a taxa de vacinação tríplice viral caiu para 92,4% nos Estados Unidos. Este índice é inferior aos 95% necessários para fornecer imunidade de rebanho, o que limita a transmissão do sarampo e protege as pessoas que não conseguem se vacinar, incluindo os recém-nascidos.

Um surto no Estado da Pensilvânia infectou mais de 1,4 mil pessoas (um número provavelmente subestimado), com sete vítimas fatais, segundo as autoridades estaduais.

O secretário de Saúde Robert F. Kennedy Jr. questionou autoridades da Pensilvânia sobre a forma de contagem das mortes por sarampo. Os CDC, no momento, se recusam a registrar algumas das mortes nos seus bancos de dados.

Em 2025, Kennedy demitiu todos os membros de um importante grupo de consultores sobre vacinação e os substituiu com pessoas nomeadas por ele próprio. Algumas delas são críticas em relação às vacinas.

O grupo recomendou diversas mudanças na vacinação, como o fim da exigência da vacina contra a hepatite B para todos os recém-nascidos. Mas um juiz federal cancelou suas recomendações.

O presidente americano, Donald Trump, também lançou dúvidas este ano sobre a segurança da vacina tríplice viral.

Trump assinou uma ordem executiva para dividir a dose em três imunizações separadas, para sarampo, caxumba e rubéola. Especialistas em saúde pública afirmam que esta mudança encarece a vacinação e poderá semear confusão sobre uma vacina já segura.

Os médicos e autoridades de saúde pública afirmam que as desinformações de Trump e Kennedy tiveram papel importante para a queda dos índices de vacinação.

"Está confundindo os pacientes. Está confundindo as famílias", segundo Gunawardhana. "Precisamos de uma mensagem clara que venha de cima."

As manobras do governo federal americano em relação às vacinas fizeram com que os Estados e as autoridades de saúde pública ocupassem o espaço, oferecendo suas próprias recomendações separadas para preservar medidas praticadas há décadas.

articles.title: Skydiving injury leaves 24-year-old tourist stranded in Australia on medical no-fly list
articles.summary: Chloe Lowe of the United Kingdom says a 10,000-foot skydiving jump in Australia left her with a damaged eardrum, an infection, vertigo and a not-fit-to-fly certificate.
articles.body: A 24-year-old tourist says she's been stranded in Australia for weeks after a skydiving jump severely damaged her eardrum, leaving doctors to declare her medically unfit to fly home. Chloe Lowe, a resident of Sheffield, United Kingdom, told the outlet NeedToKnow she's been stranded in Australia "for several weeks" after initially arriving in October for a solo birthday trip. Days before the planned three-week trip ended, Lowe went skydiving and jumped out of a plane at 10,000 feet. She damaged her eardrum and realized that, once the adrenaline wore off, she couldn't hear. CRUISE VACATION TAKES FRIGHTENING TURN AS PASSENGER IS AIRLIFTED FROM SHIP She then sought medical treatment and learned she was bleeding behind her eardrum. "I was given a not-fit-to-fly certificate and put on steroids," the influencer told NeedToKnow, a British publication. After two weeks of healing, an infection threw another wrench into her plans, leaving her in more pain and experiencing more vertigo, she said. 4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP "Turns out I now have an infection due to fluid that’s been trapped inside my ear," she said. "Every week I’m having to extend my accommodation, not knowing if I’ll be able to go home by the end of it or not." In a redacted medical certificate shared by Lowe, Queensland Health officials stated that she was admitted to Cairns Base Hospital and is "not fit to fly at this time due to the health concerns." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Lowe described herself as being "trapped on the other side of the world with no way home." Lowe told NeedToKnow she decided to visit Australia to pay respects to her grandfather, who died while scuba diving on the Great Barrier Reef in 2016. "This was a really meaningful trip for me, as I wanted to visit the place where he sadly passed away," she said. articles.title: White House drops Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination after Republicans raise concerns
articles.summary: The White House is dropping Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed Tuesday.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The White House is dropping Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed Tuesday. The decision comes a day before the Senate Health Committee was scheduled to vote on whether to advance her nomination to the full Senate for confirmation. Axios first reported the White House’s decision. The move follows weeks of doubts from key Republicans on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. To advance to the full Senate, Overton would have needed 11 votes in the 21-member committee, meaning she couldn’t afford to lose a single Republican if all Democrats opposed her. Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the committee’s chairman, had questioned whether Overton — a preventive medicine doctor who serves as a domestic policy official in the White House — had enough experience to lead the agency. Prior to joining the White House, Overton worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute. Before Overton’s confirmation hearing in September, Cassidy wrote on X that he had “strong concerns” about her nomination, saying her lack of managerial experience left her poorly prepared to lead the agency. In a post last week, Cassidy said he remained undecided. On Tuesday night, Cassidy criticized the White House for pulling Overton’s nomination. “Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. “My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.” “The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues. The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” said Cassidy, who is leaving Congress in early January. “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.” Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, told NBC News last week that she was undecided and had “not taken a position,” saying she needed “to get some answers on various things.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska declined last week to say how she’d vote. During the confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked Overton about political pressure surrounding access to mifepristone, and criticized Overton for not taking a clear position on the subject. Overton has praised the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion. The FDA is set to finish its safety review of mifepristone in March, one of the most consequential decisions the agency faces. Overton’s nomination was already working against a tight window. Democrats take control of the Senate in early January, when she would have had to be renominated if she weren’t confirmed in this Congress. Her chances of being confirmed under a Democratic-controlled Senate would be slim. The FDA has been without a permanent commissioner since Dr. Marty Makary resigned in May, in part because of the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vaping products. The vacancy adds to a long period of upheaval at the nation’s top health agencies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention went nearly a year without a permanent director after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed Susan Monarez just 29 days into the job last year. Trump’s first pick for that role, former congressman Dave Weldon, couldn’t secure enough Republican support, and the agency cycled through a series of acting leaders before the Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz in August.

articles.title: RFK Jr. faces fierce backlash after US loses measles-free status for first time in 26 years
articles.summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faces criticism after the U.S. lost measles elimination status amid over 5,400 confirmed cases this year.
articles.body: Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing mounting criticism from Democrats after the United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years. The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination designation amid a resurgence of the highly contagious virus, with more than 5,400 confirmed cases reported this year — the highest annual total in more than three decades. The virus has spread largely among unvaccinated populations, prompting criticism from Democrats who have previously scrutinized Kennedy's stance on vaccines. On Tuesday, Kennedy vowed to stop measles outbreaks and restore the country's measles elimination status, while continuing to recommend vaccination against the disease. CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status," Kennedy said in a statement. He added, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." Several Democrats sharply criticized Kennedy following the announcement. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state has reported its first measles-associated death in more than three decades, involving a child, accused Kennedy of contributing to declining vaccination rates through years of vaccine skepticism. CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK "RFK Jr. promised to 'Make America Healthy Again.' Now America has lost its measles-free status for the first time in 26 years," Hochul said. "A disgraceful display of incompetence from the nation's highest public health office," she added. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also blamed Kennedy, arguing that the loss of elimination status reflected the consequences of vaccine misinformation and skepticism. "There is a clear line from the misinformation, vaccine skepticism, and incompetence of RFK Jr. to this devastating news and very real consequences," Shapiro said. "Measles is preventable. We eliminated it in this country once, and we can do it again." MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL Another Democratic governor called for Kennedy's removal from office. "This dangerous setback was 100% avoidable and is the result of one person: RFK Jr.," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said. "Remove him now." The U.S., which had maintained the measles designation since 2000, is experiencing its worst measles outbreak since 1991 and has reported more than twice as many cases as in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Measles elimination means there has been no continuous local transmission of the virus for at least 12 months. The U.S. reached the status in 2000 after years of coordinated immunization campaigns. NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz defended the agency's response to the ongoing outbreak, emphasizing that vaccination remains the most important tool for protecting Americans. "The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said. She added that the CDC had invested approximately $100 million in state and local health departments to strengthen outbreak prevention and response. The agency also noted that MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.7% in 2023–2024. In his statement, Kennedy cited COVID-19-era disruptions as a factor in declining routine childhood vaccination coverage, noting that several other countries, including Canada, Mexico and the United Kingdom, had also lost their measles elimination status. articles.title: New organ donation rules take effect after alarming reports of patients showing ‘signs of life’
articles.summary: New HRSA organ donation rules take effect Nov. 18, adding a five-minute waiting period after circulatory death and a formal pause process for families.
articles.body: New organ donation guidelines have taken effect as of Nov. 18, updating procedures for some donors. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a branch of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), previously announced the policy update in a press release after the changes were approved by the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network in August. The new guidelines apply to donation after circulatory death (DCD), in which organs are recovered after the heart and lungs stop functioning. This differs from donation after brain death, when the donor is declared dead based on the irreversible loss of brain function. BRIDE IS WALKED DOWN WEDDING AISLE BY MAN WHO RECEIVED HER LATE FATHER'S HEART What the new rules require The changes include a formal process to pause donation if patient safety concerns arise. Families, medical providers and other people involved in the process must be told they can request a pause and how to do so. Procedures will also be added for handling and reporting unplanned pauses, along with more detailed records of neurological assessments. Additionally, a minimum five-minute waiting period will be put in place after circulation stops and before organ recovery begins. Timing concerns While the changes are intended to strengthen patient safeguards and improve communication with families, University of Rochester bioethicist Dr. Lainie Ross told NPR that allowing organ procurement teams to approach families before they decide whether to withdraw life-sustaining care could leave them feeling pressured or distrustful of doctors’ motives. In public comments, the American Society of Transplantation said it supports honoring requests to pause the donation process at any point. ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED 'SIGNS OF LIFE,' FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS Previous cases in which organ recovery was reportedly begun before confirmation of death have raised questions about safeguards in the donation process. HRSA Division of Transplantation Director Dr. Raymond Lynch told Fox News Digital that "does not happen" under the process governed by the new guidelines. "The point of these policies that were put into place is to make sure that we do preserve the sanctity of that decision and make sure that the technical parts of the operation ... pose no risk to the patient," Lynch told Fox News Digital. The HRSA director said these new guidelines improve the "safety, quality and consistency of care that's already being delivered across the United States." Organ donation has changed just within the last decade, according to Lynch. Historically, most donors were declared as "brain-dead," meaning they were "legally deceased" at the time the decision was made. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Now, we're dealing with [DCD], which means that it's an individual who's not brain-dead, but they're very severely injured," he said. "The medical team and the family have come to the decision that they're going to change the goals of care and let that person have a natural, compassionate death." "In that setting, shortly after they pass away, their organs are removed through a surgical procedure." "The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor." The guidelines do not change the roles of the patient’s healthcare team or the organ procurement organization (OPO), the group that coordinates organ donation and recovery. Rather, they set clearer expectations for when donation-related discussions and procedures take place, according to Lynch. "Historically, it was very, very late in the patient's medical course before there could be a discussion of them being an organ donor," he said. "And that really has two kinds of harm." One concern was that families may have felt "rushed or pressured" to decide whether to authorize organ donation before they had enough time to make an informed choice. He said delays could deny patients "the chance to give the gift" of organ donation, as they intended when they signed up to be donors. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The other risk was an "insufficient delivery" of information and recording of decisions, according to Lynch. He said the new guidelines bring more thorough conversations and clearer records of what information was shared with families, and when. These conversations are "happening in truly tragic circumstances," Lynch noted, as families and loved ones are feeling fear and grief. The HRSA aims to ensure that the quality and quantity of communication and medical care is "very high." "All of this is about elevating this to the level of a medical specialty," he said. "We're making sure through these regulations that there is a level of professionalism and consistency, and that the care people's loved ones are going to get is ... compassionate and respectful." What families should know Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician and Fox News medical contributor, said families should know that "there are now clearer safeguards," including the five-minute wait and the chance to pause the process. She added that while organ donation saves lives, protection of the donor "must always come first." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "I think these changes are a positive step toward improving patient safety, transparency and public trust," Widmer, who was not involved in the guideline updates, told Fox News Digital. "My concern is whether these safeguards will be consistently enforced across hospitals and organ procurement organizations." The doctor added that a policy is "only as effective as its implementation," and that additional procedural requirements don’t "unnecessarily interfere with a patient’s wishes to donate." Widmer said she'd like to see stronger national standards for independent neurological assessments and "greater oversight" of organ procurement practices. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "The medical team caring for the patient should remain completely independent of the organ recovery process," she emphasized. "Families also deserve clear explanations of exactly what will happen, including any specialized procedures used to preserve organs." "The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor."

articles.title: Antisemitism fears push Jewish med school students, providers and patients to hide faith, ADL finds
articles.summary: Jewish medical providers hide Star of David necklaces at work as the Anti-Defamation League reports a rise in antisemitism across healthcare.
articles.body: Jewish medical students, healthcare providers and patients are experiencing antisemitism, with some choosing to hide their faith out of fear of discrimination, a new report from the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) shows. "Particularly since October the 7th, we've seen an explosion of antisemitism in different fields, in different spaces, and we've been alarmed by this prevalence of anti-Jewish bias. But in particular, the trend in the healthcare and medical field is particularly pernicious," ADL CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. Greenblatt underscored the vulnerability of patients seeking care, who must trust that their providers will make the right decisions without being blinded by bias. He said that the Jewish patients' need to self-censor was "deeply troubling." JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS The ADL, along with the American Jewish Medical Association (AJMA), examined the prevalence of antisemitism in the medical field from multiple perspectives based on interviews with 40 Jewish patients across 15 states and 44 healthcare professionals — one of whom is not Jewish — with an array of roles located in 12 states. For medical school students, the ADL and AJMA used two qualitative interviews and conducted nine focus groups with 31 Jewish medical students from 14 states. The ADL and AJMA are not the first ones to note the troubling trend of increasing antisemitism in the medical field. A 2024 peer-reviewed survey of 645 self-identified Jewish medical professionals found that 39.2% reported experiencing antisemitism in the professional or academic environment, and 26.4% said they felt unsafe or threatened. Dr. Miri Bar-Halpern, who is a clinical psychologist and lecturer in psychology at Harvard Medical School, told the ADL that the findings in its report were "absolutely troubling" and that "they should worry everyone." "When Jewish doctors or medical students are being targeted, that’s going to add to the burnout. Those providers might be treating you. Those providers might be carrying this compound stress that is affecting the way that they will be able to perform in the surgery room or the way they’re engaging with the next patient," she said. Bar-Halpern also echoed Greenblatt’s concerns about patients, who are already in a vulnerable position, feeling even more unsafe. "If you cannot trust that support, and you start hiding part of who you are, you’re not only dealing with whatever health issue brought you there in the first place, but now there’s an additional layer of stress," she told the ADL. "Over time, that can really hinder people from healing, and it can add to the suffering." LEO TERRELL TAKES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S ANTISEMITISM FIGHT NATIONWIDE ON 15-CITY TOUR Participants in the ADL's report describe instances as patients in which they faced barriers to accessing kosher food and Jewish chaplains. Some said that they faced outright hostility, with one saying that a provider "turned to ice" upon finding out that the patient was Jewish. One patient said that when seeking medical help after the Oct. 7 attacks, they had an experience with a nurse who they felt was dismissive. The patient told the ADL that the nurse gave incorrect information regarding test results and "put me into a room that was completely not cleaned and smelled like urine." "I proactively took my religion off of any medical records that I could, because I didn't want to be in that situation again ... I don't want to compromise my safety," the participant said. Jewish medical providers face antisemitism both internally and from patients, according to the ADL report. It notes that Jewish healthcare providers often deal with antisemitism in small ways — wondering if they are safe to wear a Star of David, whether they can disclose their faith to a patient or even asking for Jewish holidays off. The ADL report includes stories from providers who concealed Star of David necklaces under their scrubs, hid Jewish-affirming pages on their professional websites and endured derogatory remarks from colleagues and supervisors. The organization noted that the healthcare professionals who chose to hide their faith did so not merely out of a desire for personal privacy, but also as a calculation of risk. "I wear a Jewish star, but I always leave it under my shirt at work," one participant told the ADL. "As soon as I leave work, I'll always take my star out. But there was one day in particular where I didn't notice that my star was outside of my shirt, and a colleague actually came up to me and said, 'Hey, put that in your shirt, right?' And it wasn't meant negatively, but it was more meant ... I think of protection." Another participant, who identifies as Jewish and is part of the LGBTQIA+ community, described hiding a "Jewish affirming therapist page" on their website out of fear that patients might reject them over their faith. "I have the two identities ... I'm queer, I'm also Jewish, and I work with the queer community, but if they see I'm Jewish, they might not work with me, and that's just the reality," the participant said. INSIDE ONE UNIVERSITY'S EFFORTS TO RECLAIM THE CLASSROOM AND FIGHT ANTISEMITISM In his discussion with Fox News Digital, Greenblatt called out two medical community groups in particular: Healthcare Workers 4 Palestine (HCW4P) and Doctors Against Genocide (DAG), both of which are openly anti-Israel, as sources of antisemitism in the medical field. The ADL noted in its report that HCW4P's posts included praise of U.S.-designated terror groups, such as Hamas, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and Palestinian Islamic Jihad. Additionally, the report states that in December 2023, just weeks after the Oct. 7 attacks, DAG issued a "call to action" against the Israel-Hamas war at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C. The event, according to the ADL report, was canceled following "public backlash." "Now, I think it's coming from within the field itself, in part because of the existence of anti-Zionist activist groups," Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. "We saw groups like Healthcare Workers 4 Palestine — this is a thing — or Doctors Against Genocide that have mobilized healthcare workers within the anti-Israel movement. And I think what we need to recognize is that, again, when a group of medical professionals is doing something like praising the founders of Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad, medicine and patient care are not really on their agenda." "Doctors are supposed to take the Hippocratic oath, but all you actually have is hypocrisy when medical professionals are cheering terror organizations who murder civilians," he added. "It's not normal, it's not okay, and professional bodies have an obligation to respond." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The ADL report also recorded antisemitism in medical schools, with Jewish medical students describing self-censoring and exclusion. One participant said that, while at a program, someone pointed at his Star of David necklace and said, "He loves genocide!" Greenblatt pointed to the increasing antisemitism in undergraduate programs, and said that seeing a similar pattern in graduate schools was "even more problematic." "This is an environment where the students are supposed to be more experienced, older and wiser, simply put, more mature," Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. "The institutions themselves are supposed to have much less tolerance for sort of errant behavior. You expect a higher degree, again, of maturity and, if you will, professionalism when you're in the graduate school environment." Some Jewish medical students who spoke with the ADL said their reluctance to share their faith began before they entered their graduate studies. The report notes that participants recalled "deliberately minimizing or omitting their Jewish identity from their applications" out of fear that an admissions reader's views on Jews or Israel could harm them. Greenblatt called for a "detox campaign to detox the discrimination and undo the bias that's becoming embedded in medical schools and, again, healthcare more generally." For the ADL and AJMA, that means urging institutions to adopt their "Top Five Asks for Hospitals and Healthcare Institutions." These items include explicitly naming antisemitism, including anti-Zionist harassment, as prohibited conduct; building accessible and confidential reporting systems for patients, staff, students and trainees; requiring trainings on antisemitism and Jewish identity; supporting Jewish inclusion structures, such as employee resource groups; and adopting and applying a robust religious accommodations policy. Greenblatt emphasized that the "Five Asks" are not aimed at "special treatment for Jewish people, but equal treatment." "I mean, in reality, it's not hard ... to remember we're all created in the image of God and recognizing our fellow men and women's just basic humanity, demonstrating a degree of decency and empathy," Greenblatt told Fox News Digital. "It's just, generally speaking, a good best practice for all of us to observe, particularly for Jewish people in a moment when, again, they're seeing such a rise of antisemitism and feeling so much hate." articles.title: 3 Easy Exercises To Instantly Lower Stress and Tension in the Body, From a Trainer
articles.summary: Work always comes with stressors, but your blood pressure doesn’t have to stay spiked all day long. Turn to these 3 exercises to ease your stress.
articles.body: Stress at work is inevitable, but that doesn’t mean calm is completely out of reach. Consider the obligatory meeting, for example — whether you’re presenting, learning difficult news or being tasked with even more assignments — it can spike your blood pressure, which can lead to feeling flushed, headaches, heart palpitations and a hefty dose of sweat, according to the Cleveland Clinic. But the emotional distress you encounter throughout the day doesn’t have to stay with you all day. Mental Health Tip of the Day: Lower Your Blood Pressure With These Exercises Start TODAY trainer and TODAY contributor Stephanie Mansour shared three moves you can do to tackle stress fast: Why It Matters Temporary blood pressure spikes are caused by several things, including strong emotions, according to the Cleveland Clinic. While it’s normal for your blood pressure to fluctuate throughout the day, it can be uncomfortable. So, it’s helpful to know how to return it to its normal state, allowing your blood to flow as it should and your body to adapt to the sudden surge in anxiety and panic. How to Get Started After a stressful event, Mansour recommended performing these three exercises in order. Shrug Your Shoulders: Draw your shoulders up to your ears and then drop them down. “This helps to relieve chronic muscle tension and also loosen up your neck,” said Mansour.Breathe: Next, “take a slow, deep breath in,” Mansour instructed. “Hold it at the top for four seconds, and then slowly breathe out.” The practice is a quick meditation, she said.Smile: For five seconds, “plaster” a smile on your face, said Mansour. “Train your brain that it’s time to move on to happier thoughts.” TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Palestinians flee refugee camp as Israel begins operation in central Gaza
articles.summary: At least three Palestinians were killed as Israeli forces launched strikes near a refugee camp.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have killed three Palestinians during a new operation in central Gaza on Wednesday, according to hospital officials.

Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground reported that Israeli tanks were operating near Salah al-Din Street, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij camp.

An Israeli air strike targeted the town of al-Mughraqa, north of Nuseirat, killing one person and wounding several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera.

Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary said many Palestinians were fleeing areas in central Gaza as the Israeli operation got under way.

“We have been seeing people in eastern parts of Maghazi and Bureij, and people who are close to Salah al-Din starting to evacuate and flee the area due to the fact that there were huge explosions heard, live ammunition, and artillery shelling in that area,” Khoudary said.

“The Israeli forces in their announcement did not issue an evacuation order for people who are living in this area. They just mentioned that there is a military operation that is going to start, they are going to destroy the infrastructure and they are going to start demolishing in this area,” she added.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Israeli army said the operation aimed to “eliminate a threat” to its forces operating in the area of the “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the Israeli-occupied area of Gaza, and was established under the “ceasefire” agreement signed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025.

In a statement, the Israeli military said: “We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip.”

Hamas condemned the Israeli operation as a “flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”.

“Forced evacuation orders and the displacement of citizens carried out under the threat of violence and bombardment constitute a war crime and a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law,” the group said in a statement.

“The occupation’s actions are aimed at herding citizens into a narrow strip of the Gaza Strip, further exacerbating the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe,” it added.

Hamas said it holds Israel and the United States responsible for “the repercussions of the military operation and the crimes committed against civilians”.

Before the announcement of the Israeli operation, two Israeli drone attacks on Gaza killed at least two people, hospital officials told Al Jazeera.

Al-Shifa Hospital reported that one person was killed and others were wounded in an attack on the Sheikh Ijlin neighbourhood in southwestern Gaza City.

In a separate attack, Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital reported that one person was killed in Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, where the hospital had earlier reported an injury.

Earlier on Wednesday, Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that hospitals had recorded seven deaths and received 15 wounded people in the previous 24 hours.

Six people were killed by Israel over that period while one died from injuries caused by an earlier attack, the ministry said.

articles.title: ‘Batkid’ Who Went Viral in 2013 Is Starting College! See Him All Grown Up in New Pic
articles.summary: It’s been 13 years since ‘Batkid,’ a 5-year-old boy with leukemia named Miles Scott, saved the city of San Francisco in an elaborate Make-a-Wish event.
articles.body: When he was just 5 years old, Miles Scott donned a cape and teamed up with Batman to save the city of San Francisco, which had transformed into Gotham. Nicknamed “Batkid” at the time, Scott had been diagnosed with leukemia at just 18 months old and was in remission during the massive Make-A-Wish day. Now, 13 years later, Scott, 18, is cancer-free, in his first year of college and looking back on the moment that brought a city together, Make-A-Wish Bay Area wrote in a Facebook post. The elaborate event was a nearly citywide takeover thanks to the help of Ed Lee, the late mayor of San Francisco. The San Francisco police and fire departments, the San Francisco Giants and thousands of caped volunteers also helped Scott’s wish come to life, Make-A-Wish recalled on the 10-year anniversary. That day even inspired a 2015 documentary called “Batkid Begins.” “I feel like it brought hope to more than just a couple people,” Scott said of the viral moment. “They came out and were happy. It wasn’t just about me on that day. It was about getting all together and just having fun.” An estimated 11,000 to 12,000 volunteers aided in making the day a reality, according to an NBC Bay Area estimate. That included actors, stage crew members and more. Scott now works part-time at his local irrigation district, the Facebook post notes, and he’s also studying to become a certified welder. Outside of work and school, Scott likes to go snowboarding and hunting. He also continues to get yearly screenings for lymphoblastic leukemia, a type of cancer that affects the white blood cells. It’s a type of cancer that more often affects children and young people, but is often treatable thanks to advances in medicine over the last decade, as TODAY.com reported previously. For more than a decade now, Scott’s screenings have shown him to be cancer-free.
